This exemption from 510(k) requirements, subject to certain limitations, is immediately in effect for such devices. This exemption will decrease regulatory burdens on the medical device industry and will eliminate private costs and expenditures required to comply with certain Federal regulations. FDA is amending the classification language within the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) for certain class II clinical toxicology test systems to reflect this final determination. articles.title: Medical Devices; Immunology and Microbiology Devices; Classification of the High Throughput DNA Sequencing for Hereditary Cancer Predisposition Assessment Test System
articles.summary: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is classifying the high throughput DNA sequencing for hereditary cancer predisposition assessment test system into class II (special controls). The special controls that apply to the device type are identified in this order and will be part of the codified language for classification of the high throughput DNA sequencing for hereditary cancer predisposition assessment test system. We are taking this action because we have determined that classifying the device into class II will provide a reasonable assurance of the safety and effectiveness of the device. We believe this action will also enhance patients' access to beneficial innovative devices, in part by reducing regulatory burdens.

Atlantic Highly Migratory Species; Atlantic Bluefin Tuna Fisheries; General Category October Through November Quota Transfer and Adjustment
articles.summary: NMFS is adjusting the Atlantic bluefin tuna (BFT) General category October through November 2026 time period subquota by transferring 70.2 metric tons (mt) of quota from the Reserve category. Simultaneously, NMFS is adding 16.7 mt of subquota remaining from the June through August time period to the General category October through November time period. This action results in a total adjusted General category October through November time period subquota of 192.9 mt and an adjusted Reserve category of 42 mt. This action would affect Atlantic Tunas General category (commercial) permitted vessels and Highly Migratory Species (HMS) Charter/Headboat permitted vessels with a commercial sale endorsement when fishing commercially for BFT.

articles.title: Air Plan Approval; GA; Removal of Nonattainment Area New Source Review
articles.summary: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or Agency) is approving a State Implementation Plan (SIP) revision submitted by the State of Georgia through the Georgia Environmental Protection Division (EPD) on June 27, 2024. The revision removes permitting requirements related to nonattainment, including nonattainment new source review (NNSR), from Georgia's SIP as obsolete, removes certain provisions related to the use of emission reduction credits (ERCs), and makes other changes based upon the lack of any areas designated as nonattainment for the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) in Georgia. The EPA is approving these changes pursuant to the Clean Air Act (CAA or Act).

articles.content: Hurricane Isaias: Category 3 Threat to Gulf & Supply Chain - FreightWaves Hurricane Isaias is intensifying in the Gulf, threatening to become a Category 3 storm and unleash significant damage across the Southeast. We break down the storm’s projected path, its potential impact on critical infrastructure like refineries and ports, and what freight and logistics operators can expect for trucking capacity and diesel prices. Stay ahead of the storm’s supply chain disruptions with our full analysis. Hurricane Isaias, currently a Category 1 storm, is forecast to strengthen to a Category 2 by Wednesday and potentially reach Category 3 with winds of up to 100 miles per hour before making landfall Friday around 2 p.m., according to a FreightWaves Sonar analysis. The storm’s projected path stretches from just east of Houston across to the Florida Panhandle, encompassing major freight corridors and energy infrastructure in the Gulf Coast region. The most consequential supply chain risk lies in the energy sector. Up to six refineries sit in the storm’s path, and Gulf State refineries collectively account for 50% of the nation’s refining capacity — a total of 18.2 million barrels per day. Offshore production operators are already sending home nonessential workers, though output continues normally for now. articles.content: Sanctioned 22-Year-Old Tanker Makes Rare Late-Season Arctic Voyage Oil tanker along Northern Sea Route in July 2025. (Source: Atomflot) Sanctioned 22-Year-Old Tanker Makes Rare Late-Season Arctic Voyage Malte Humpert Total Views: 178 October 7, 2026 A 22-year-old product tanker sanctioned by the European Union is making an unusual late-season voyage along Russia’s Northern Sea Route, highlighting the growing use of older, lower-specification vessels to move petroleum products through the Arctic. The Dakar, a 21,300-dwt oil and chemical products tanker built in 2004, is carrying methyl tert-butyl ether (MTBE), a gasoline additive, and appears to be heading west along Russia’s Arctic coast, according vessel tracking data. The cargo was loaded onto another vessel in China in August before being transferred to Dakar off Yeosu, South Korea, in September. Dakar is not an Arctic-specialist tanker, but vessel data from S&P Global indicates that it does have an ice-class designation. That distinguishes it from non-ice-class tankers, while placing it well below the Arc4 and higher ice-class vessels purpose-built for regular Arctic operations. The distinction is increasingly relevant as Russia’s shadow fleet expands its presence on the Northern Sea Route. Advocacy group Bellona identified 50 shadow-fleet oil tankers on the NSR between the start of the 2026 summer-autumn navigation season and mid-September, compared with 38 during the entire 2025 season. articles.summary:

The post The Costs You Can’t See in Packaged Goods Supply Chains appeared first on FreightWaves.
articles.content: The Costs You Can't See in Packaged Goods Supply Chains - FreightWaves Packaged goods supply chains are full of examples of exception requests, like when a retailer asks for a custom pack configuration, a key account needs a special label, or a shipment gets rerouted on short notice to hit a delivery window. Those kinds of exceptions aren’t necessarily problems on their own. Exception handling can look like good customer service. But on Oct. 15, FreightWaves and G3 Logistics are asking what happens when you stop counting those requests one at a time and start adding them up. That’s the topic of The Hidden Cost-to-Serve in Packaged Goods: Managing Rework, Specialized Handling, and Operational Exceptions, a free webinar that will dig into the repack jobs, relabeling work, retailer-specific requirements, and expedited changes that accumulate inside packaged goods networks until they’re no longer exceptions at all. Without visibility into what those exceptions cost, they can be devastating to margins over time. G3 Logistics brings transportation, warehousing, and supply chain expertise to a common packaged goods challenge: customer requests that add work beyond the standard flow. A package change, relabeling request, or tighter delivery window can affect handling, schedules, inventory, and capacity across multiple teams. articles.content: JP Morgan-backed NOCC expands China car carrier programme - Splash247 CIMC Raffles JP Morgan-backed Norwegian Car Carriers (NOCC) has expanded its newbuilding programme in China, adding another pair of 7,100 ceu ships at CIMC Raffles. Shipbuilding sources place the latest vessels at the group’s Yantai Raffles facility for delivery in 2030, extending a relationship that has already produced four LNG dual-fuel car carriers for the Oslo-based tonnage provider. The latest pair would take NOCC’s confirmed programme with CIMC Raffles to six ships. However, shipbuilding databases seen by Splash indicate the programme could be larger still. In addition to two 7,100 ceu units listed as hulls 641 and 642 for delivery in 2030, the databases show another two ships, hulls 651 and 652, against NOCC for delivery in 2030 and 2031. Those additional two units have not been disclosed by NOCC and could represent options attached to the latest contract. NOCC’s own fleet list has yet to reflect any of the latest additions and currently shows only the four ships from its earlier series. The first two, NOCC Pacific and NOCC Adriatic, have already entered service. CIMC Raffles delivered the latter in January this year. The remaining ships from that original programme, NOCC Kattegat and NOCC Skagerak, are due next year. articles.content: Commodity trader takes Pelagic handysize for up to 11 months - Splash247 Pelagic Partners Cyprus-based shipowner and fund manager Pelagic Partners has fixed its handysize bulker UBC Houston to an unnamed major commodity trader for up to 11 months. The 2015-built, 39,000 dwt vessel has secured a nine-to-11-month time charter at $17,250 per day, Pelagic said. The company did not identify the charterer. The Chengxi Shipyard-built bulker forms part of the Pelagic Yield Fund and trades in the UBC Pool. Pelagic acquired the vessel in June 2023 as part of an expansion of its dry bulk exposure. At the time, the acquisition took the fund compartment holding the ship to seven vessels and Pelagic’s total acquired fleet since inception to 18 units. The latest fixture gives Pelagic medium-term cover while leaving the ship open again next year. At the headline rate, the contract represents roughly $4.7m to $5.8m of gross hire over the nine-to-11-month window before commissions, off-hire and other deductions. Pelagic’s wider shipping investment platform has also been active in dry bulk this year. In July, Oslo-listed Pelagic Credit struck a $47.4m sale-and-leaseback deal covering three Hartmann-controlled handysize bulkers, its first investment in the sector. The ships were placed on seven-year bareboat charters back to Hartmann. articles.content: $100B Trade Gap: China vs. US Data Exposed - FreightWaves Ends Tomorrow - Promo Code: FALLFORF3 Join us at F3: Future of Freight Festival, October 27 & 28th Register Now × A staggering $100 billion discrepancy exists between China’s reported exports and the US’s recorded imports. Michael Kanko, CEO of ImportGenius.com, explains what this trade data delta signifies for the global supply chain. He details how granular shipping records are used for everything from sourcing new components to ensuring compliance with international sanctions, and why transparency in air cargo data is the next big battle for US manufacturers. ImportGenius has identified a more than $100 billion gap between what China reported shipping to the United States last year and what U.S. records show as received — a discrepancy that highlights the limitations of relying on government trade statistics alone and the growing role of bill-of-lading data in supply chain intelligence. The finding emerged when ImportGenius normalized its shipment-level data into TEUs — the standard 20-foot equivalent unit used in global container trade — and cross-referenced that count against U.S. Census dollar values to derive a value-per-container figure. Comparing that metric to China’s own TEU-normalized figures produced what the company described as a major and “mystifying” difference. The 56-year-old master mariner, founder of ShipGod AI, spends 25 years with China Yangtze Shipping, rising from deck cadet to …
articles.content: ShipGod AI: Why every vessel needs its own digital memory - Splash247 After four decades at sea and ashore, Bing Hou has reached a simple conclusion about shipmanagement: too much of what keeps vessels safe still depends on paper, spreadsheets and what individual seafarers happen to remember. The 56-year-old master mariner, founder of ShipGod AI, spends 25 years with China Yangtze Shipping, rising from deck cadet to Class-1 ocean-going master and serving on everything from containerships and tankers to LNG carriers, passenger ships and offshore vessels. Since 2016, Hou has worked ashore in marine management, ship surveying, DPA roles and teaching. Across all of it, he says one problem keeps resurfacing. “The paper never really changed,” he tells Maritime CEO. “ISM got the principle right decades ago: every ship must operate its own Safety Management System, fitted to that specific ship. But in practice, the documents that keep ships safe still live in binders, spreadsheets and memory.” The result, he argues, is a steady leakage of institutional knowledge. Records are often completed after events, while valuable operating experience can disappear whenever officers sign off. “The turning point for me was watching how much time good officers spend managing documents instead of being officers, and how much of what they know is never captured for the next crew,” Hou says. Uber announced Tuesday that it has agreed to acquire Boston-based ezCater in an all-cash transaction that will combine the company’s workplace catering business with Uber Eats and Uber for Business. The deal gives Uber access to a large pool of higher-value, scheduled deliveries generated by corporate meetings, employee meal programs and events, according to a news release. EzCater generated more than $2.5 billion in gross bookings during the trailing 12 months, growing in the high teens year over year. The company is profitable on a non-GAAP operating income basis and is expected to be margin accretive to Uber. Its average order value exceeds $400. The platform allows businesses to order from more than 140,000 restaurants nationwide and provides tools for companies to manage ordering and food spending. For Uber (NYSE: UBER), the acquisition provides another way to put commercial delivery volume through its existing network while expanding its B2B business. articles.content: New Jersey CDL school lawsuit questions evidence behind FMCSA shutdown - FreightWaves Start CDL Inc. is challenging its emergency removal from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration’s training registry. The Cinnaminson, New Jersey-based truck driving school said the FMCSA improperly used drivers’ later English-proficiency violations to justify shutting down its federally regulated training operations, according to a complaint filed Oct. 2. But the 236-page complaint and exhibit packet presents questions beyond that legal dispute: A six-driver spreadsheet names another training provider, the attached roadside reports concern 10 different drivers, and a scanned removal notice makes substantive findings against a third school. The school’s own account also contains unresolved date discrepancies, including an English-assessment certificate dated after the roadside inspection it allegedly preceded. Start CDL filed the suit Oct. 2 in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey against the U.S. Department of Transportation, FMCSA and Administrator Derek D. Barrs, seeking reinstatement and relief from the agency’s action. FMCSA’s Aug. 31 notice immediately removed Start CDL from its training provider registry, along with more than 100 other schools. The notice to shutdown arrived as federal regulators crack down on hundreds of commercial driver training providers and attempt to create stricter enforcement of CDL training. articles.content: U.S. Container Imports Slow After Stronger-Than-Expected Summer The Pier 300 channel at the Port of Los Angeles. Photo courtesy Port of Los Angeles U.S. Container Imports Slow After Stronger-Than-Expected Summer Mike Schuler Total Views: 50 October 8, 2026 U.S. container imports are finally beginning to slow after an unusually long peak shipping season that stretched through the summer and into early fall, according to the latest Global Port Tracker report from the National Retail Federation (NRF) and Hackett Associates. The slowdown comes after months of stronger-than-expected cargo volumes at major U.S. ports, as retailers continued bringing in merchandise despite tariffs, inflation and higher transportation costs. Ports covered by Global Port Tracker handled 2.3 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in August, up 0.4% from July but down 0.7% from a year earlier. August now appears to have been the busiest month of 2026, marking a shift from last month’s forecast that September would take the top spot. “Even with any fluctuations in final data, we’re likely past the busiest part of the year,” said Jonathan Gold, NRF vice president for supply chain and customs policy. “The truth is that the peak season started early and was stretched out through the summer and early fall, with the difference from month to month often amounting to little more than a rounding error,” Gold said. Shipments were virtually unchanged at $658.6 billion, the first stall after eight monthly gains. New orders rose 0.1% to $663.5 billion. The ratio of unfilled orders to shipments rose to 6.87 from 6.81. Census does not adjust the figures for inflation. Orders for motor vehicle bodies, parts and trailers rose 0.8%. Machinery orders rose 1.1%. Nondefense capital goods orders excluding aircraft rose 1.6%. Durable goods orders fell 0.1%, with transportation equipment down 0.7% and nondefense aircraft and parts down 4.3%. articles.content: AI gold rush transforms trans-Pacific trade and logistics - FreightWaves The artificial intelligence infrastructure boom is creating significant new trade flows and opportunities for third-party logistics providers and carriers. Freight transportation companies are rapidly scaling up capabilities, especially to support semiconductor supply chains in Asia, the epicenter for production and distribution of advanced chips used to power AI applications, data centers, connected devices and next-generation vehicles. Two reports issued on Wednesday show how AI-related goods such as semiconductors and data-transmission equipment have become a major driver of international trade growth, spawning increasingly complex regional and global supply chains that depend on speed, visibility, cross-border expertise and resilience. Unlike traditional consumer electronics, AI infrastructure requires the coordinated movement, including customs clearance and storage, of oversized, high-value and highly sensitive equipment from manufacturers across Asia to hyperscale data centers under construction around the world. Semiconductors, data transmission equipment and data center hardware accounted for 42% of all goods trade growth in 2025, and that share rose to about 76% during the first quarter, according to an annual report on globalization trends by the New York University Stern School of Business, and commissioned by DHL Group. OK By Oh Seok-min SEOUL, Oct. 8 (Yonhap) -- South Korea is strictly enforcing its export controls on Russia, the foreign ministry said Thursday, stressing that no exports of commercial petroleum products to Russia have been confirmed through customs clearance procedures. Currently, South Korea prohibits exports of strategic items to Russia and subjects an additional 1,402 non-strategic items that could potentially be used for military purposes to case-by-case export authorization, according to the ministry. "The controlled items are determined through interagency discussions after comprehensively considering their potential military use, economic impact and international coordination," the ministry said in an explanatory note jointly issued by the industry ministry and the customs agency. Outbound shipments to Russia dropped to US$4 billion in 2025 from $10 billion in 2021 as South Korea joined international efforts to maintain peace through export controls "despite the economic burden on companies and the public," the ministry noted. (c) REUTERS/Edgard Garrido Mexican Auto Exports Slump in September as US Tariffs Take Toll Reuters Total Views: 116 October 8, 2026 By Sarah Morland MEXICO CITY, Oct 8 (Reuters) – Mexico’s auto exports posted their biggest slump so far this year, data from statistics office INEGI showed on Wednesday, a decline analysts attributed to tariff policies from the US, the biggest market for the Latin American country’s top industrial sector. Mexico auto exports fell 12% in September compared to a year earlier, the steepest decline since December 2025, while monthly output slumped 15%. Domestic sales, however, increased 8%, helping buffer the pain for the key manufacturing industry. The data comes as government officials review the US-Mexico-Canada free trade pact, but even with talks continuing, Mexican cars still face tariffs of 25%. Mexican officials estimate that complying with rules that stipulate using North American-sourced parts brings the burden down to 10% to 12%. articles.content: Almi Marine founder Evgenia Daskalopoulou dies - Splash247 Almi Marine Management Greek shipowner Evgenia Daskalopoulou, founder and president of dry bulk outfit Almi Marine Management, has died. Almi announced her death on Wednesday, saying she passed away surrounded by her family. Daskalopoulou was born in 1958 and founded the Athens-based company in 1992. She built Almi from a small dry bulk operation into a modern supramax and ultramax owner and manager. Greek shipping records show the company started out with two 1970-built handysize bulkers. “More than that, she shaped its character,” Almi said in announcing her death, highlighting her emphasis on integrity and respect for staff both ashore and at sea. The company said operations would continue as normal and that the Daskalopoulou family and management team remained committed to carrying on the business. Almi currently manages six bulkers totalling 365,140 dwt — three supramaxes and three 64,000 dwt ultramaxes. Its fleet includes the 2024-built Mea Mare, Spike and Subra, alongside the older Altus, Anima and Sole. The company has also been building up its future fleet. In February, Almi signed for two 64,000 dwt ultramaxes at Nantong COSCO KHI Ship Engineering, or NACKS, for delivery in the second quarter of 2029. articles.content: Macquarie reveals $99m Technomar boxship refinancing - Splash247 Technomar Macquarie has disclosed a $99m senior debt facility for George Youroukos-led Technomar covering the refinancing of seven containerships. The Australian financial group said the funding was provided to shipowning entities within the Athens-based Technomar Group, although it did not identify the seven vessels, disclose pricing or give the maturity of the facility. The transaction forms part of a growing Greek shipping book at Macquarie, which has deployed more than $2bn in the market since completing its first deal with Atlas Maritime in 2017. Its current Greek shipping portfolio exceeds $1bn across more than 75 transactions. Macquarie has completed more than 25 transactions with Atlas alone and has also been building relationships with newer Greek names. The financier revealed that it backed Adele Shipmanagement’s first bulker acquisitions and now finances four ships for the company. Technomar, established by Youroukos in 1994, remains heavily weighted towards containerships while also managing dry bulk tonnage. Current vessel-registry data links the company to a fleet approaching 100 managed ships. The owner has a long track record of buying secondhand boxships. Splash previously tracked Technomar picking up tonnage from German owners during an earlier phase of container fleet expansion, including a pair of 7,849 teu post-panamaxes acquired from Zeaborn. articles.content: Namura absorbs Imari steel arm ahead of shipbuilding expansion - Splash247 Namura Japan’s Namura Shipbuilding is absorbing its wholly owned Imari Steel Center as the shipbuilder moves to tighten control of production ahead of a major expansion of its newbuilding business. The Osaka-listed builder has approved the merger, with the transaction scheduled to take effect on April 1, 2027. Namura will remain the surviving company and Imari Steel Center will be dissolved. Imari Steel Center sits next to Namura’s main Imari yard in Saga prefecture and handles the upstream steel functions supporting vessel construction, including unloading, sorting, storage, processing and quality assurance of shipbuilding plate. Namura said combining the operations should speed up decision-making, allow better deployment of personnel and other resources, improve manufacturing efficiency and help with recruitment and training as the group increases newbuilding output. The internal reshuffle comes as Namura embarks on one of its biggest capacity pushes in years. Japan’s transport ministry last month approved up to ¥49.9bn ($319m) of government backing for an investment programme involving Namura and subsidiary Hakodate Dock, part of Tokyo’s wider drive to rebuild domestic shipbuilding capacity. articles.content: U-Ming doubles down in China with six-ship bulker spend - Splash247 U-Ming Taiwan’s U-Ming Marine Transport has committed up to $312m on six more bulkers in China, adding four ultramaxes and firming another pair of Newcastlemaxes as it presses ahead with plans to build a 100-ship fleet. Two separate Taiwan exchange disclosures from U-Ming’s Singapore subsidiary put the combined investment at between $296m and $312m. The larger ships are two 211,000 dwt newcastlemaxes at Jiangsu Hantong Ship Heavy Industry, priced at between $77m and $80m each for a total of $154m to $160m. The filing follows U-Ming’s June contract at the same yard for two firm ships plus two options at exactly the same price range. The latest two-ship disclosure matches the optional pair attached to that deal, taking the Hantong programme to four firm units. U-Ming is also paying between $142m and $152m for four 64,000 dwt ultramaxes at Sumec Marine-controlled New Dayang Shipbuilding, equating to $35.5m to $38m per ship. The first of the ultramaxes is scheduled for delivery in the fourth quarter of 2029, with the remaining three following during 2030. The latest contracting advances an expansion plan approved by U-Ming earlier this year covering four 210,000 dwt bulkers and four ultramaxes. Greek shipping sources report that the Athens-based owner has booked three 64,000 dwt bulkers at COSCO Shipping Heavy Industry’s Zhoushan yard, with delivery scheduled for 2030. The fresh deal follows Almi’s return to the newbuilding market in February after a four-year absence. Managing director Christos Hadjigeorgiou confirmed at the time that the company had signed for two 64,000 dwt next-generation ultramaxes at Nantong COSCO KHI Ship Engineering, or NACKS, for delivery in the second quarter of 2029. The latest Zhoushan trio takes Almi’s known forward programme to five 64,000 dwt newbuilds across two COSCO-linked yards. The owner already has close ties with the Chinese-Japanese NACKS and DACKS yards, taking three ultramaxes from DACKS in 2024. Almi currently controls six bulkers. Its fleet renewal has also included the disposal of older supramax tonnage, including the 2008-built Anasa. For a price marker, Splash noted in August that Xclusiv was assessing a standard Chinese-built ultramax at around $36m, which would put three ships at roughly $108m if Almi contracted near prevailing levels. The package forms part of QatarEnergy’s wider redevelopment of the mature Maydan Mahzam oil field. The latest award follows another large Maydan Mahzam contract handed to PetroVietnam Technical Services Corporation (PTSC) in September. PTSC has not officially disclosed the contract value, although Vietnamese media reports put it at around $3bn. Maydan Mahzam is located around 110 km northeast of mainland Qatar and has been producing since 1965. articles.content: Oil exports surge back through Hormuz despite mounting attacks - Splash247 IMO Oil flows from the Middle East have climbed back above pre-war levels even as attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz accelerate to their fastest pace since the conflict with Iran erupted on February 28. Provisional Kpler data shows regional crude exports exceeded pre-war volumes on four days during the final week of September, reaching between 19.5m and 22.5m barrels per day. The seven-day moving average stood at 18.5m barrels per day on October 1, compared with an average of around 18m barrels per day in the year before the war. The numbers cover Hormuz and Red Sea movements as well as terminal exports and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. LNG cargoes exiting Hormuz also rose in September to their highest monthly level since February. The recovery is providing a powerful cargo base for tanker markets, although brokers caution that improving logistics could eventually erode some of the extraordinary inefficiencies that have propelled rates. “For dirty tankers, higher Gulf crude exports and the return of Yanbu provide firm underlying cargo demand,” Sentosa Shipbrokers noted, adding that more efficient logistics could gradually reduce STS activity and unwind part of the “exceptional inefficiency premium” supporting VLCC earnings. articles.content: Japan targets 35 shadow fleet ships in first vessel sanctions - Splash247 Greenpeace Japan has imposed sanctions directly on individual vessels for the first time, targeting 35 ships linked to Russia’s shadow fleet as Tokyo steps up efforts to restrict Moscow’s oil-export network. The measures took effect on October 2 under Japan’s Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act. Japanese companies will now need government permission to provide specified services to the 35 vessels and for capital transactions, including loans and debt guarantees, connected with their sale, purchase, lease or charter. Japan’s foreign ministry has identified all 35 ships by IMO number. A limited transition applies to contracts concluded before October 2, but only where the relevant obligations or services are completed before November 1. The restrictions cover services including ship repairs and insurance. It is the first time Tokyo has placed vessels themselves under sanctions, bringing Japan closer to the approach already adopted by the UK and European Union against ageing tankers moving Russian oil outside mainstream Western shipping, finance and insurance channels. The shipping measures formed part of a wider package that also froze the assets of 33 Russian organisations and nine individuals and introduced export restrictions against four entities in Turkey and the UAE. articles.summary:
Dotra Compliance, an AI-driven platform built to serve as a carrier's "virtual compliance department," is helping small and midsize carriers close the gap between regulatory volume and in-house resources. articles.content: A Virtual Compliance Department for Every Fleet - FreightWaves Ask carriers what’s changed about trucking compliance lately, and you’ll likely hear about the accumulation of new rules that change faster than most back offices can absorb them. David Vincent has had a front-row seat to that accumulation. He’s co-founder of Visionary Ventures, the technology company that built and operates Dotra Compliance, a platform designed to serve as what Vincent calls a virtual compliance department. FreightWaves sat down with Vincent to talk through where carriers are losing ground and where a software layer can realistically help. He laid out a picture of an industry squeezed from multiple directions at once, including a faster enforcement, a Supreme Court ruling that rewrote how brokers vet carriers, and a volume of paperwork that outpaces small compliance departments. The current compliance environment, Vincent says, feels more difficult than it used to because it is. Carriers have been dealt a stretch of regulatory change that would challenge any safety department. “In the last 18 months alone, carriers have absorbed English proficiency becoming an out-of-service violation, revoked ELDs, a non-domiciled CDL crackdown, a new FMCSA registration system and a Supreme Court ruling that changed how brokers choose carriers,” Vincent said. (Source: Novatek) EU Imports Record 12.18 Million Tonnes of Russian Arctic LNG Malte Humpert Total Views: 113 October 9, 2026 Europe’s estimated bill reaches €7.88 billion through September as U.S. sanctions deadline adds uncertainty for Yamal’s specialized tanker fleet. The European Union imported a record 12.18 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas from Russia’s Yamal Arctic project in the first nine months of 2026, paying an estimated €7.88 billion, according to an analysis by German environmental group Urgewald. Shipments rose 9.5% compared with the same period last year, even as Yamal’s worldwide deliveries fell 1.3%. Europe received 167 cargoes, accounting for 85% of the project’s recorded deliveries by volume, according to Urgewald’s analysis of Kpler shipping data. The figures highlight Europe’s continuing importance to Russia’s Arctic gas trade despite the EU’s planned phaseout of Russian LNG imports. The bloc’s estimated bill included €2.88 billion in the first quarter, €3.08 billion in the second and €1.92 billion in the third. Third-quarter deliveries fell 13.6% year-over-year to 2.21 million tons. September shipments, however, reached 792,440 tons, slightly above the same month last year, with an estimated value of €818 million. articles.content: Black Sea grain exports crater amid widening maritime war - Splash247 Ambrey Black Sea wheat exports are plunging at the height of the traditional shipping season as escalating attacks on commercial vessels and port infrastructure leave both Russia and Ukraine struggling to get their harvests to international markets. Fresh vessel-tracking data compiled by AXSMarine and published by Greek shipbroker Ursa show wheat loadings across the Black Sea slumped to just 1.6m tonnes in September, 77.8% below the 7.3m tonnes recorded in the same month last year. September volumes were also down 45.6% from August, with shipments falling to their lowest September level since 2017. The collapse is particularly striking given that August and September are normally among the busiest months for Black Sea grain exports as the new harvest comes to market. Across the first nine months of 2026, Black Sea wheat loadings reached 36.3m tonnes, down 12.2% year-on-year and the second-lowest January-to-September total since 2017. The deterioration comes as the maritime war spreads well beyond the immediate approaches to Russian and Ukrainian ports, increasingly threatening alternative grain export corridors. Earlier this week, the Turkish-owned general cargo ship Royad Mammadov, carrying corn from Ukraine’s Danube port of Izmail to Italy, sank following a drone attack in Romania’s exclusive economic zone, killing two seafarers. articles.content: Trøim-backed Bruton opens review amid VLCC sale talk - Splash247 Nor-Shipping Tor Olav Trøim-backed VLCC owner Bruton has launched a strategic review after market speculation over a potential transaction, with International Seaways linked by shipbroking sources to the purchase of at least two of its remaining newbuildings. The Oslo-listed company acknowledged the speculation on Thursday, saying it had started a review aimed at maximising shareholder value. Bruton declined to identify any potential counterparties or elaborate on what form a transaction could take, stressing that there was no certainty a deal would materialise. Market talk has International Seaways negotiating for at least two ships, with the most obvious candidates being the 300,000 dwt Mount Frontier and Mount Summit under construction at New Times Shipyard. The vessels are due in August and October 2027 and, unlike Bruton’s first two VLCCs, have yet to secure employment. Bruton’s latest fleet list shows both without charter coverage. Brokers have circulated numbers north of $200m apiece for the pair. Neither Bruton nor International Seaways has confirmed negotiations or pricing. Bruton’s own investor material lists the yard price of Mount Frontier and Mount Summit at about $117m each.
